families.stem: Morgan invests $\text{R{=P}}$ into an account which pays out a lump sum at the end of ${=n}$ years. If he gets $\text{R{=fixed(A, 2)}}$ at the end of the period, what compound interest rate did the bank offer him? The interest is compounded annually. Give the rate as a percentage per annum, as a number without the % sign.
solution: Write down what is given: $A=\text{R{=fixed(A, 2)}}$, $P=\text{R{=P}}$, $n={=n}$ and $i=\,?$
Write down the formula and substitute the known values: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$ gives $\text{R{=fixed(A, 2)}}=\text{R{=P}}(1+i)^{{=n}}$
Divide both sides by $\text{R{=P}}$ to get the bracket on its own: $\frac{{=fixed(A, 2)}}{{=P}}=(1+i)^{{=n}}$
Take the $n$th root of both sides (here $n={=n}$) and use your calculator: $1+i=\sqrt[{=n}]{\frac{{=fixed(A, 2)}}{{=P}}}={=fixed(g, 2)}$
Subtract $1$ from both sides to find $i$: $i={=fixed(g, 2)}-1={=fixed(r / 100, 2)}$
Write the rate as a percentage: $i\times 100={=r}$, so the bank offered a compound interest rate of ${=r}$ % p.a.
Check: $\text{R{=P}}\times({=fixed(g, 2)})^{{=n}}=\text{R{=fixed(A, 2)}}$, which is the amount Morgan received.

Parameters were enumerated with exact fractions so that every instance is clean: the basic family always gives whole-rand balances and difference (96 combinations); the advanced family gives 173 valid combinations with margins that make the nearest-rand answer insensitive to ordinary intermediate rounding. The solution templates use fixed(x, 2) strings for decimals (e.g. 0.05, 1.05) because I could not confirm how the engine renders a decimal Fraction; the advanced family also uses string literals inside a let expression for the winning-bank sentence. mc:g10m9s3-1-3:compound-better-for-everyone concerns borrowing, which is outside the book's investment context, so no family uses it; mc:g10m9s3-1-3:bigger-rate-wins is not attached because neither family is mcq.

families.context: Sipho wants to invest a lump sum today at a fixed compound interest rate (a whole-number percentage per annum) so that it grows to a target amount in rand after 2 years. Only the rate and the target amount change between instances; the target is always chosen so that the amount to invest is a whole number of rand, so no rounding is needed.

params.why: the target amount must be a whole number of rand, so that the principal comes out exact

families.stem: Sipho wants to invest some money at a compound interest rate of ${=r}$ % p.a. How much money should he invest if he wants to reach a sum of $\text{R{=amt}}$ in ${=n}$ years' time?
solution: Read the question carefully and write down the given information: $\begin{aligned}A&=\text{R{=amt}}\\P&=?\\i&=\frac{{=r}}{100}={=fixed(r / 100, 2)}\\n&={=n}\end{aligned}$
To find the amount he must invest, make $P$ the subject of the formula: $\begin{aligned}A&=P(1+i)^{n}\\\frac{A}{(1+i)^{n}}&=P\end{aligned}$
Substitute the values and calculate: $\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\text{R{=amt}}}{(1+{=fixed(r / 100, 2)})^{{=n}}}\\&=\text{R{=prin}}\end{aligned}$
Sipho must invest $\text{R{=prin}}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: n = 2 only, whole-number rate, and the target is built backwards from a round principal (a multiple of lcm(base, 500) where base = 100^n / gcd(100^n, (100+r)^n)), so A is a whole number and the principal is an exact whole number of rand. This removes the book's 'round up' step on purpose (the book's own questions round up, e.g. 24001.46 -> 24002), which is what the standard and advanced work covers. Exact arithmetic means the key cannot differ by calculator rounding. Example: r = 4, principal 2500 -> A = 2704 (2704 / 1.0816 = 2500). Likely student errors (not used as distractors, since the item is numeric): multiplying A by (1+i)^n instead of dividing, dividing by 1+i once instead of (1+i)^n, or dividing by 1 + n*i (simple-interest habit).

families.context: Naledi needs one sum of money in rand after a few years (for a laptop) and a second sum after a longer time (for a course). She will invest two separate amounts today, one for each need, both at the same compound interest rate (a percentage with one decimal place, per annum). Each principal is found with the book's method P = A / (1 + i)^n, rounded up to the next whole rand as in the book's own exercises, and the two rounded amounts are added.

params.why: keep the first principal well away from a whole rand, so rounding up is unambiguous
keep the second principal well away from a whole rand, so rounding up is unambiguous

families.stem: Naledi needs $\text{R{=amt1}}$ for a laptop in ${=n1}$ years' time and $\text{R{=amt2}}$ for a course in ${=n2}$ years' time. She will invest two separate amounts today, one for each need, at a compound interest rate of ${=fixed(rate, 1)}$ % p.a. How much must she invest in total? Round each of the two amounts up to the next whole rand before you add them, and do not round any other value.
solution: Each need has its own investment, so work out the two amounts separately. For the first need write down the given information: $\begin{aligned}A_1&=\text{R{=amt1}}\\P_1&=?\\i&=\frac{{=fixed(rate, 1)}}{100}={=fixed(iv, 3)}\\n_1&={=n1}\end{aligned}$
Make $P$ the subject of the formula: $\begin{aligned}A&=P(1+i)^{n}\\\frac{A}{(1+i)^{n}}&=P\end{aligned}$
First amount: $\begin{aligned}P_1&=\frac{\text{R{=amt1}}}{(1+{=fixed(iv, 3)})^{{=n1}}}\\&=\text{R{=fixed(pv1, 2)}}\end{aligned}$ This rounds up to $\text{R{=q1}}$.

Second amount, with $A_2=\text{R{=amt2}}$ and $n_2={=n2}$: $\begin{aligned}P_2&=\frac{\text{R{=amt2}}}{(1+{=fixed(iv, 3)})^{{=n2}}}\\&=\text{R{=fixed(pv2, 2)}}\end{aligned}$ This rounds up to $\text{R{=q2}}$.
Add the two rounded amounts: $\text{R{=q1}}+\text{R{=q2}}=\text{R{=total}}$
Naledi must invest $\text{R{=total}}$ in total.
families.notes: Advanced = several steps: the book's P = A / (1+i)^n applied twice (different n for each need) and the results added. The rounding follows the book ('round up' means ceiling: its own answers 24001.46 -> 24002 and 44871.03 -> 44872 only fit that reading). The stem says each amount is rounded UP to the next whole rand BEFORE adding, which fixes the order of rounding and the direction. Both unrounded principals are computed exactly (rational arithmetic), and each is required to have a fractional part between 0.1 and 0.9, so the ceiling is never decided by a near-integer value or a calculator's last digit. The rate is a one-decimal percentage with a non-zero last digit (8.1 to 14.9, as in the book) so it always prints cleanly with fixed(rate, 1); i prints with fixed(iv, 3). n1 is 2 to 5 and n2 is at least n1 + 2 and at most 9, so every instance has two different periods and no '1 years' wording. Amounts are multiples of R100, as in the book. Worked example: rate 11.8, A1 = R30000 at n1 = 2 gives 24001.46 (as in the book, ex9-2-5), which rounds up to 24002. This is a reviewer note only: a solver who rounds intermediate powers of (1+i) could lose accuracy, hence the 'do not round any other value' sentence in the stem.

families.context: Thandi buys a fridge on hire purchase. She pays no deposit, the whole cash price is repaid over a whole number of years with simple interest, and a fixed insurance premium is added to every monthly payment.

params.why: the monthly repayment must not fall exactly on a half cent, so rounding to the nearest cent is unambiguous
keeps the insurance premium realistically small next to the monthly repayment (at most half of it)

families.stem: Thandi buys a fridge on hire purchase. The cash price of the fridge is $\text{R{=cash}}$. She pays no deposit and pays the fridge off over ${=yrs}$ years at an interest rate of ${=r}\%$ p.a., charged as simple interest. An insurance premium of $\text{R{=prem_t}}$ is added to every monthly payment. Calculate Thandi's monthly payment in rand, correct to the nearest cent.
solution: There is no deposit, so the amount financed is the cash price: $P = \text{R{=cash}}$. The interest rate is $i = {=i_t}$ and the period is $n = {=yrs}$ years.
Calculate the accumulated amount: $A = P(1 + in) = {=cash}(1 + {=i_t} \times {=yrs}) = \text{R{=acc_t}}$.
The agreement runs for ${=yrs} \times 12 = {=m}$ months, so the monthly repayment on the hire purchase agreement is $\frac{{=acc_t}}{{=m}} = \text{R{=inst_t}}$ (to the nearest cent).
Add the insurance premium to the monthly repayment: $\text{R{=inst_t}} + \text{R{=prem_t}} = \text{R{=tot_t}}$.
Thandi's monthly payment is $\text{R{=tot_t}}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the book's we08 method (A = P(1 + in), divide by the number of months, add the premium) with the deposit removed and the term a whole number of years, so n needs no conversion from months. Simple interest is stated in the stem so a blind solver cannot reach for compound interest; the book leaves it implicit. Cash price is a multiple of R100 so A is a whole number of rand. Premium is in 5-cent steps (R10.00 to R35.00) and is kept at no more than half the monthly repayment. Tie check keeps the repayment off an exact half cent; because the premium is an exact number of cents, rounding the repayment first (as the book does) and rounding the sum give the same answer. I checked 20 000 sampled instances against an independent step-by-step calculation that rounds as the book does: they agree, about 99.5% of draws are accepted, and answers run from about R57 to R560. Typical errors to watch for in review or blind solves: adding the premium once instead of to every month, dividing by the number of years instead of months, using compound interest. No misconceptions are catalogued for this objective and a numeric family has no distractors to tag, so none are proposed.

families.context: Zodwa buys a laptop on hire purchase. She pays a percentage of the cash price as a deposit, repays the balance over a number of months that is not a whole number of years, with simple interest, and a fixed insurance premium is added to every monthly payment.

params.why: the accumulated amount must be a whole number of cents, so no intermediate rounding can change the answer
the monthly repayment must not fall exactly on a half cent, so rounding to the nearest cent is unambiguous
keeps the insurance premium realistically small next to the monthly repayment (at most half of it)

families.stem: Zodwa is buying a laptop on hire purchase. The cash price of the laptop is $\text{R{=cash}}$. She has to pay a ${=d}\%$ deposit and then pay off the remaining amount over ${=m}$ months at an interest rate of ${=r_t}\%$ p.a., charged as simple interest. An insurance premium of $\text{R{=prem_t}}$ is added to every monthly payment. Calculate Zodwa's monthly payment in rand, correct to the nearest cent.
solution: The deposit is ${=d}\%$ of the cash price: ${=d}\% \times {=cash} = \text{R{=dep}}$. The amount that is financed is $P = {=cash} - {=dep} = \text{R{=P}}$.
Write down the interest rate and the period in years: $i = {=i_t}$ and $n = \frac{{=m}}{12} = {=n_t}$.
Calculate the accumulated amount: $A = P(1 + in) = {=P}(1 + {=i_t} \times {=n_t}) = \text{R{=acc_t}}$.
Calculate the monthly repayment on the hire purchase agreement: $\frac{{=acc_t}}{{=m}} = \text{R{=inst_t}}$ (to the nearest cent).
Add the insurance premium to the monthly repayment: $\text{R{=inst_t}} + \text{R{=prem_t}} = \text{R{=tot_t}}$.
Zodwa's monthly payment is $\text{R{=tot_t}}$.
families.notes: Harder variant of the book's ex9-3-10: a percentage deposit comes off the cash price first, the term is given in months and is an odd multiple of 6 (18, 30, 42 or 54), so n is a decimal (1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5 years), and the rate moves in half-percent steps (6% to 21%), so i can be a three-decimal number such as 0.125, as in the book's ex9-7-26. Simple interest is stated in the stem. Cash price is a multiple of R100 and the deposit is a multiple of 5%, so the deposit and the amount financed are whole rand. Two requires keep it clean: the accumulated amount A is an exact number of cents (about 70% of draws pass), and the monthly repayment is not an exact half cent, so the book's round-then-add and a full-precision solution always agree. The premium is in 5-cent steps (R10.00 to R35.00) and at most half the repayment. I checked 20 000 sampled instances against an independent calculation that rounds as the book does: they agree, and the formula reproduces the book's ex9-3-10 (P = 5778, i = 0.08, n = 3 gives A = 7164.72). Answers run from about R49 to R603. Typical errors to watch for in review or blind solves: applying the percentage to the wrong base, using n = 30 instead of 2.5 in A = P(1 + in), forgetting the deposit, adding the premium once. No misconceptions are catalogued for this objective and a numeric family has no distractors to tag, so none are proposed.

families.context: The price of popcorn and a cooldrink at the movies is known today. The average rate of inflation over the past few years is given, and the student finds how many rand the price has risen by over that period (past price first, then the difference).

params.why: the rate is a decimal such as 9.2 or 7.3, never a whole percentage, as in the book's own harder examples
keeps the cent digit away from a rounding boundary, so rounding the past price first or the difference last gives the same answer

families.stem: The price of popcorn and a cooldrink at the movies is now $\text{R{=now}}$. The average rate of inflation over the past ${=n}$ years was $\text{{=rt}}$ % p.a. By how many rand has the price increased over these ${=n}$ years? Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
solution: First find what the popcorn and cooldrink cost ${=n}$ years ago. Write down the given information: $A=\text{R{=now}}$, $P=?$, $i=\frac{{=rt}}{100}=\text{{=it}}$, $n={=n}$.
Today's price is the amount $A$. Use the compound interest formula and make $P$ the subject: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$, so $P=\frac{A}{(1+i)^{n}}$.
Substitute and calculate: $P=\frac{{=now}}{(1+{=it})^{{=n}}}=\frac{{=now}}{({=gt})^{{=n}}}=\text{R{=pt}}$.
The increase is today's price minus the price ${=n}$ years ago: $\text{R{=now}}-\text{R{=pt}}=\text{R{=dt}}$.
families.notes: Advanced = several steps plus the book's decimal-rate twist (ex9-4-7 uses 9.2 %, ex9-4-6 uses 7.3 %). The student must work BACKWARDS (make P the subject, divide by (1+i)^n) and then take a difference. Rounding is robust: today's price is a multiple of R5, so (today - past price rounded to cents) equals (exact difference rounded to cents); the second require removes instances where the exact value sits within 0.05 of a cent boundary. Worked instance: now=60, n=5, 9.2 % -> past price R38.64 (the book's own ex9-4-7 value), increase R21.36. Rate range 6.1 %-13.9 %, never a whole percent. The misconception catalogue for this objective is empty, and a numeric family carries no distractors, so none is proposed; the typical slips (multiplying by (1+i)^n instead of dividing, or stopping at the past price) give visibly wrong numbers.

families.context: The price of a bag of potatoes is known from some years ago, not from today. The inflation rate is constant, and the student finds the price some years from now, so the price grows for the sum of the two periods.

params.why: a student who rounds today's price to the cent before growing it further must reach the same final cents
keeps the final value away from a rounding boundary

families.stem: A bag of potatoes cost $\text{R{=p0}}$ ${=n}$ years ago. If the rate of inflation is $\text{{=r}}$ % p.a. from then on, how much will a bag of potatoes cost ${=m}$ years from now? Round only your final answer to 2 decimal places.
solution: Write down the given information: $P=\text{R{=p0}}$ (the price ${=n}$ years ago), $A=?$, $i=\frac{{=r}}{100}$.
The price grows from ${=n}$ years ago to ${=m}$ years from now, so it grows for $n={=n}+{=m}={=tot}$ years in total.
To determine the future cost we use the compound interest formula: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$.
Substitute and calculate: $A=\text{{=p0}}\times\left(1+\frac{{=r}}{100}\right)^{{=tot}}=\text{R{=at}}$.
families.notes: Advanced = the twist that the starting price is not today's price. The student must see that the compounding period is (years ago) + (years ahead) and not just the years ahead. A student who first finds today's price and then grows it reaches the same answer, because the stem says to round only at the end and the second-to-last require rejects any instance where rounding today's price to the cent would change the final cents. Same method as ex9-4-2: A = P(1+i)^n with whole-number rates, now with a longer n (4 to 11). Worked instance: P=15, n=3, m=3, 12 % -> 15 x 1.12^6 = R29.61, which is the book's ex9-4-2 value. Answers stay below about R165. The misconception catalogue for this objective is empty, and a numeric family carries no distractors, so none is proposed.

records.notes: Only the advanced tier was listed as a gap, so two advanced families were written and nothing for basic or standard. They cover two different twists: (1) work backwards for the past price, then take a difference, with a decimal rate; (2) the given price is from the past, so the compounding period is the sum of years ago and years ahead. Both use only the book's own formula, A = P(1+i)^n, and its rearrangement for P. I did not write a changing-rates or a find-the-rate or find-the-years family, since those need methods this objective does not teach. The misconception file for this objective is empty, and both families are numeric (no distractors), so none is proposed. Slug prefixes are increa and pastfu. I computed the rounding checks and the acceptance rates for both parameter sets outside the engine: about 81 % of draws pass for the first family and about 58 % for the second. I did not run the family engine itself, so please run the standard family check on both.

families.context: The population of a small town grows at a constant average percentage rate each year.

params.why: the unrounded population must be a whole number, so the entry-level answer is exact

families.stem: The current population of a small town is ${=P}$ and the average rate of population growth is ${=r}$ % p.a. Use the compound interest formula to calculate what the town council can expect the population to be in ${=n}$ years' time.
solution: Write down the known values: $P={=P}$, $i=\frac{{=r}}{100}$, $n={=n}$ and $A=?$
Write down the compound interest formula: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$
Substitute the values: $A={=P}\left(1+\frac{{=r}}{100}\right)^{{=n}}$
Calculate: $A={=A}$
The town council can expect the population to be ${=A}$ in ${=n}$ years' time.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: one application of A = P(1+i)^n with n = 2 or 3. P is a multiple of 400 (n = 2) or 8000 (n = 3) and the rate is 5, 10, 20 or 25 %, so the result is always an exact whole number and no rounding is asked. Integrality is enforced by a require. 64 distinct instances. Model: worked example 11 (page 346): same known-values, formula, substitute, answer layout. The stem names the compound interest formula so a blind solver cannot read the growth as simple (linear) growth.

families.context: The population of a town grows at a constant average percentage rate each year.

params.why: the swapped-rate-and-years distractor must differ from the correct option

families.stem: The population of a town is currently ${=P}$ and the average rate of population growth is ${=r}$ % p.a. Which calculation uses the compound interest formula correctly to find the expected population of the town in ${=n}$ years' time?
solution: The compound interest formula is $A=P(1+i)^{n}$, where $P$ is the starting amount, $i$ is the rate per year written as a fraction of $100$ and $n$ is the number of years.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Uses the rate as a whole number
proposed_misconceptions.description: Puts the growth rate into the formula as r (for example 1 + 5) instead of r/100 (1 + 0.05), so the percentage is never converted to a fraction.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Treats population growth as simple growth
proposed_misconceptions.description: Adds the same amount every year, P(1 + i x n), instead of multiplying by (1 + i) each year, so growth is not compounded.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Swaps the rate and the number of years
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the number of years as the percentage and the percentage as the exponent, because both are just numbers in the question.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaves out the 1 in (1 + i)
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the growth rate i alone as the yearly multiplier, P x i^n, forgetting that the population keeps what it already had and adds the growth.

families.notes: Basic: setting up the compound interest calculation without evaluating it. mcq is natural here because the four distractors are the four classic set-up errors (rate not divided by 100, simple instead of compound growth, rate and years swapped, missing the 1). The stem holes (P, r, n) differ between instances, so distinct_by_choices is not needed. r != n is required so the swapped option never equals the correct one. The objective has no catalogued misconceptions; the four ids above are proposed.

families.context: The population of a city grows at a constant average percentage rate each year.

params.why: keep the unrounded population at least 0.05 away from a .5 boundary so the rounded answer is unambiguous

families.stem: The current population of a city is $\text{{=m}\ {=t}\ {=u}}$ and the average rate of population growth is ${=rate}$ % p.a. Use the compound interest formula to calculate by how many people the population is expected to increase over the next ${=n}$ years. Do not round off until your final answer, and round that to the nearest integer.
solution: Write down the known values: $P=\text{{=m}\ {=t}\ {=u}}$, $i=\frac{{=rate}}{100}={=i3}$, $n={=n}$ and $A=?$
Write down the compound interest formula: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$
Substitute the values: $A=\text{{=m}\ {=t}\ {=u}}\left(1+{=i3}\right)^{{=n}}$
Calculate, rounding only at the end: $A={=Afix}$
Round to the nearest integer: $A\approx{=Ar}$
The increase is the future population minus the current population: ${=Ar}-{=P}={=inc}$
The population is expected to increase by about ${=inc}$ people over the next ${=n}$ years.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own twist from exercise 9.5 question 3 (page 347), where the answer is the increase A - P, not the new population. Adds three things beyond the standard book question: a rate with a decimal (0.4 to 2.8 %), a seven-digit population, and the final subtraction. P is built from millions, thousands and units parts (each of the last two 100 to 999) so the stem prints it in the book's spaced style without leading-zero problems. The exact value is computed in integers (top / bottom); the require keeps its fractional part at least 0.05 from .5, and the stem forbids intermediate rounding, so a calculator solver agrees. Rounding A then subtracting P gives the same integer as rounding A - P because P is an integer. Book check of the formula: 3 879 090 x 1.011^6 = 4 142 255 (page 347). Increases range from about 43 thousand to 1.96 million.

families.context: Bridget, a South African shopper, wants to buy an iPod priced in pounds (£) and pays in rand (R). The rand cost is the price in pounds multiplied by the exchange rate, the number of rand in £1. She compares the rand cost at the current exchange rate with the rand cost after the rate has dropped.
families.stem: Bridget wants to buy an iPod that costs $\text{£ }{=p}$, with the exchange rate currently at $\text{£1}=\text{R}{=r1}$. In a month the exchange rate drops to $\text{£1}=\text{R}{=r2}$. How much will she save, in rand, if she buys the iPod at the new rate instead of at the current rate?
solution: The cost in rand is the price in pounds multiplied by the exchange rate.
At the current rate: $\text{Cost}={=p}\times\text{R}{=r1}=\text{R}{=c1}$.
At the new rate: $\text{Cost}={=p}\times\text{R}{=r2}=\text{R}{=c2}$.
The rate has dropped, so the iPod now costs less and the difference is a saving: $\text{Saving}=\text{R}{=c1}-\text{R}{=c2}=\text{R}{=saving}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Subtracts the rates but never multiplies by the price in pounds
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds how far the exchange rate moved (old rate minus new rate) and gives that as the saving or loss, forgetting that the item costs many pounds and each pound is affected by the change.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gives the rand cost at the new rate as the saving or loss
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student computes the price in rand at the new rate and stops there, instead of subtracting it from (or taking it away from) the rand cost at the old rate to find the difference.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Divides the pound price by the exchange rate
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student converts pounds to rand by dividing the price in pounds by the number of rand per pound instead of multiplying, so the rand costs and the saving come out wrong.

families.notes: Basic entry point of the skill, modelled on ex9-6-1b (Bridget's iPod, saving when the rate drops). Strips the book's extra 'she estimates' sentence so the learner meets only the two rates: rand cost at the current rate, rand cost at the lower rate, subtract. Direction is always a drop, so the answer is a positive saving. Ranges: price 20 to 150 pounds in steps of 5, current rate R10 to R20, new rate 1 to 6 below it and never under R7 (the book's rates run R9 to R20). Saving is a whole number between 20 and 900 rand. Wording 'compared with buying at the current rate' is explicit so a blind solver cannot read the saving against any other rate. A numeric family has no distractors, so the proposed misconceptions describe the wrong numbers a marker might see (r1 - r2, p * r2, p / r1 - p / r2). Standard (the book's own three-rate exercises) and advanced tiers were not requested; the book has no exercise harder than a single comparison, so no advanced family was written.

The rate has risen, so the television now costs more and the difference is a loss: $\text{Loss}=\text{R}{=c2}-\text{R}{=c1}=\text{R}{=loss}$.

proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds how far the exchange rate moved (old rate minus new rate) and gives that as the saving or loss, forgetting that the item costs many pounds and each pound is affected by the change.

proposed_misconceptions.description: The student computes the price in rand at the new rate and stops there, instead of subtracting it from (or taking it away from) the rand cost at the old rate to find the difference.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Divides the pound price by the exchange rate
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student converts pounds to rand by dividing the price in pounds by the number of rand per pound instead of multiplying, so the rand costs and the saving come out wrong.

families.notes: Basic entry point, the mirror of fall-saving, modelled on ex9-6-2c (Mthuli's television, loss when the rate moves up). The book pairs every 'save' part with a 'lose' part, and the learner has to see that a rising rate makes the purchase dearer, so the same two rand costs are now subtracted the other way round. Direction is always a rise, so the answer is a positive loss. Ranges: price 20 to 150 pounds in steps of 5, current rate R8 to R15, new rate 1 to 6 above it and never over R20. Loss is a whole number between 20 and 900 rand. The book's extra 'he estimates the rate will drop' sentence is left out so the only rates in the stem are the two being compared. Wording 'instead of at the current rate' pins the comparison for a blind solver. Numeric family, so the proposed misconceptions describe wrong numbers (r2 - r1, p * r2, p / r1 - p / r2).

records.notes: Two basic families, one per direction of the objective (saving when the rate drops, loss when it rises). No misconceptions were catalogued, so three were declared in proposed_misconceptions; numeric families carry no distractors, so they only describe the wrong numbers a marker might see. Standard and advanced tiers were not requested: all nine book questions are standard and use one skeleton (two rand costs, subtract), and the book has no exercise harder than that, so no advanced family was written. The book's decoy sentence (the estimated drop in the loss questions) is deliberately omitted because it makes 'lose' ambiguous for a blind solver (relative to the current rate or to the estimate). I could not run the family checker or the engine, because only the two packet files were open to me, so templates, bounds and constraints are unvalidated by the tool.

families.context: A student is buying the same textbook online. One shop in the UK prices it in pounds and one shop in the USA prices it in dollars. Shipping is ignored. The two exchange rates (rand per pound and rand per dollar) are given, and the student converts both prices to rand to find the cheaper offer.

params.why: The two rand amounts must be close enough that the comparison needs the conversion, but never a tie and never wildly apart.

families.stem: Lerato wants to buy a textbook online. A shop in the UK sells it for $\text{£}{=p}$ and a shop in the USA sells it for $\text{\textdollar}{=d}$. Ignore shipping costs. Use the exchange rates $\text{£}1=\text{R}{=fixed(r / 100, 2)}$ and $\text{\textdollar}1=\text{R}{=fixed(s / 100, 2)}$. Convert each price to rand and decide which shop is cheaper. What is the cost, in rand, of the cheaper offer? Give your answer to the nearest cent.
solution: To compare prices quoted in different currencies, convert each price to rand first. Cost in rand = cost in the foreign currency $\times$ exchange rate.
UK shop: $\text{£}{=p}\times\text{R}{=fixed(r / 100, 2)}=\text{R}{=fixed(uk, 2)}$.
USA shop: $\text{\textdollar}{=d}\times\text{R}{=fixed(s / 100, 2)}=\text{R}{=fixed(us, 2)}$.
Compare the two amounts in rand: $\text{R}{=fixed(lo, 2)}$ is less than $\text{R}{=fixed(hi, 2)}$, so the shop whose price converts to $\text{R}{=fixed(lo, 2)}$ is the cheaper one.
The cheaper offer costs $\text{R}{=fixed(lo, 2)}$.
families.notes: Basic entry point of the objective: two prices, two rates given in the stem, no shipping fee, whole-number foreign prices so each conversion is an exact two-decimal rand amount (no rounding ambiguity). Skeleton follows ex9-7-37 (and the same method as ex9-6-4b and ex9-6-5) without their decimal prices or shipping twist. Numeric rather than mcq on purpose: a two-option comparison is a coin flip and cannot carry three diagnosable distractors, while asking for the rand cost of the cheaper offer still forces the student to convert both prices and decide; a student who compares the printed numbers (mc:g10m9s5-1-3:compare-without-converting) or who picks the dearer offer (mc:g10m9s5-1-3:converts-then-picks-largest) reports the wrong rand figure. The pound rate is always above the dollar rate and the prices are built so the two rand amounts are within R2 to R25 of each other, so in roughly half the instances the larger printed number is the cheaper offer. The solution never names the shop (the expression language is not assumed to have string literals); it identifies the cheaper offer by its rand amount. Worked check: p=17, r=1689, s=1243, k=1 gives d=24, UK R287.13, USA R298.32, answer 287.13. Note for the reviewer: the printed solution of ex9-6-4b uses R14.31 for the pound where the table says R14.13 (the figure R84.78 is consistent with 14.13), so that is a typo in the book, not a rate to copy.

records.notes: Only the basic tier was listed as a gap and no families existed, so one family was written. The standard and advanced tiers are already covered by the book's own questions (ex9-6-4b standard; ex9-6-4a, ex9-6-5, ex9-7-37 advanced) and were not padded with further families. No distractors are used (numeric answer), so no misconception ids are attached and none are proposed.
